deep.reconstruction:
Context (my reconstruction from this page and its neighbours). Two Gaussian integers are fixed, M = A+Bi and m = a+bi. Write p = x+yi and P = X+Yi with M p = m P, i.e. (p, P) runs along a complex line in R^4.

Solving M p = m P for two real coordinates in terms of the other two gives the two denominators:
- If y and Y are integers, solve for x and X. The determinant is δ = Ab − aB = −Im(M·conj(m)).
- If y and X are integers, solve for x and Y. The determinant is α = aA + bB = Re(M·conj(m)).

The non-integral coordinates are rounded to the nearest integer. Their fractional parts are written as x^0/δ, X^0/δ (classes 1–2) or x^0/α, Y^0/α (classes 3–4), so |x^0|, |Y^0| < α/2 (respectively δ/2). The resulting Gaussian integer t+ui = ±(M p' − m P') (up to a unit) is the object of study. A sign ε is attached to it by a rule depending on the signs of α, x^0, Y^0 and the parity of t+u.

This is the set-up of a Gauss-lemma / lattice-point argument for the biquadratic (quartic) character. It extends Gauss's third proof of quadratic reciprocity to Z[i].

Numerical example (deduced by me from the previous page's table: x^0 = −bt+au, X^0 = −Bt+Au with the rows (1−3i; −7, 9), (2i; 6, −2), (1−i; −1, 7), (1; 2, 6)). The values are a = 3, b = −2, A = −1, B = −6, so M = −1−6i (norm 37) and m = 3−2i (norm 13). Then M·conj(m) = 9 − 20i, so α = 9 and δ = 20.

Part 2) Θ' is the set of θ' arising in class 2, after normalising the sign. It consists of all T'+V'i with −bT'+aV' and −(−BT'+AV') = BT'−AV' positive and < δ/2. This parallels the previous page's description of Θ: −bT+aV and −BT+AV positive and < δ/2.

The tables 'In unserm Falle':
- Θ = {1, 1+i, 1+2i}, with ε = +1, −1, +1.
- Θ' = {i, 2i, 3i, −1+i, −1+2i, −1+3i}, with ε = −1, +1, −1, +1, −1, +1.
- Θ'' = {2−i, 3−i}, with ε = +1, −1.
- Θ''' = {1, 2}, with ε = −1, +1.

The side note 'Hier ist Θ = −*M + *m, Θ' = −*M − *m, …' records which sign/unit combination of M and m produces each family. Here * stands for an unspecified integer multiplier.

The ε-columns show a pattern, checked by me against the tables:
- In Θ and Θ'', ε = −1 exactly when θ is divisible by 1+i (T+V even).
- In Θ' and Θ''', ε = +1 exactly when θ is divisible by 1+i.

Part 3°: y and X integers. Let x', Y' be the nearest integers to x and Y. Put p' = x'+yi and P' = X+Y'i, so p−p' = p^0/α and P−P' = P^0/α with p^0 = x^0 and P^0 = iY^0. Since Mp = mP:

  i(t+ui) := Mp' − mP' = −(Mp^0 − mP^0)/α = (−M x^0 + i m Y^0)/α.

With M = A+Bi and m = a+bi, comparing real and imaginary parts gives:
- αt = −Bx^0 + aY^0
- αu = Ax^0 + bY^0

Inverting (using α = aA+bB):
- x^0 = −bt + au
- Y^0 = At + Bu

Rule: ε = −1 when α > 0, x^0 > 0, Y^0 > 0 and t+u even, etc.

Sign normalisation of t+ui:
- +θ'' if x^0 > 0, Y^0 > 0
- +θ''' if x^0 > 0, Y^0 < 0
- −θ'' if both are negative
- −θ''' if x^0 < 0, Y^0 > 0

A marginal 'besser' column proposes the alternative labels +θ', −θ''', −θ', +θ''. The next page keeps the first scheme.

With this normalisation, θ'' = T+Vi always has −bT+aV > 0 and AT+BV > 0, and θ''' has −bT+aV > 0 and −AT−BV > 0, all below α/2. This matches the next page's description of Θ'' and Θ'''.

Conclusion stated (for α > 0): every θ'' divisible by 1+i has ε = −1, and every θ''' divisible by 1+i has ε = +1. The next page completes this: an indivisible θ''' has ε = −1.

Checks on the next page's class-3 rows (mine):
- y=0, X=1 gives x = 13/9 and Y = −20/9, so x^0 = 4, Y^0 = −2, t+ui = 2 (a θ''').
- y=1, X=2 gives x^0 = −3, Y^0 = −3, t+ui = −3+i, θ'' = 3−i.

Both agree with the formulas. Overall the four families are the lattice points in open 'half-period' parallelograms. Counting them, weighted by ε, is meant to give the quartic residue symbol.
errors: Minor notational slips: on line 4 (−(−BT'+AU')) the variable U' should be V'. The same U/V confusion (and later I for T) recurs on adjacent pages.

The 'besser' column on this page proposes an alternative labelling (+θ', −θ''', −θ', +θ''). As written it would clash with θ', which is already used for class 2. The next page ignores it, so it reads as an abandoned alternative, not an error in the main line.

No mathematical errors found. The linear relations, their inversion (determinant α = aA+bB) and all four tables are correct for M = −1−6i, m = 3−2i. The enumerations of Θ, Θ', Θ'', Θ''' are complete; I checked them by bounding the lattice points. The ε-rule is consistent with every table entry, although its definition is not on this page and so cannot be independently verified.

results.what: Rounding the points of the line Mp = mP (M, m Gaussian integers) to nearest lattice points. The deviations are expressed as the linear system αt = −Bx^0 + aY^0, αu = Ax^0 + bY^0, with α = Re(M·conj(m)) (and δ = −Im(M·conj(m)) in the other classes).
results.modern_name: Gauss-lemma / lattice-point (Eisenstein-type) approach to the quartic residue symbol in Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844, Gauss-lemma style proofs of biquadratic reciprocity); the lattice-point idea goes back to Gauss's 3rd proof of QR (1808) and Eisenstein's geometric proof (1844)

results.what: Description of the sets Θ, Θ', Θ'', Θ''' as all Gaussian integers T+Vi with two linear forms (e.g. −bT+aV and ±(AT+BV) or ±(BT−AV)) lying in (0, α/2) or (0, δ/2). Each set is the lattice points of an open parallelogram (half-system).
results.modern_name: half-system / fundamental-parallelogram lattice point sets in Gauss's lemma for Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's lemma for Z[i]: Eisenstein; later expositions in Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws, ch. 6

results.what: Empirical sign rule: ε = −1 for θ'' divisible by 1+i, ε = +1 for θ''' divisible by 1+i (when α > 0). On the Θ and Θ' tables, ε depends only on the parity of T+V.
results.modern_name: parity (1+i)-divisibility rule for the sign factor in a quartic Gauss lemma

results.what: Inversion of the 2×2 integer linear system relating (t,u) and (x^0,Y^0).

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss announced but never published a proof of biquadratic reciprocity. The Nachlass is known to contain fragments of such work (parts printed in Werke II, VIII and X). This page develops a Gauss-lemma / lattice-point style computation in Z[i], with a worked example (M = −1−6i, m = 3−2i). That approach is usually associated with Eisenstein's 1844 proofs. It is notable as unpublished working detail. However, Gauss's possession of this general strategy is plausible and partly documented, and the page is a computational sketch with no completed theorem. Hence a modest score.
